confounds: Diagnosed users averaged approximately 620 retained posts versus 530 for controls. Raw post counts therefore exaggerate group differences; analyses emphasized per-user rates, user prevalence, and a first-100-post sensitivity check.
Controls showed more public-topic, political, sports, laughter, and exclamation content, suggesting collection, community, demographic, or activity-composition differences.
Clinical vocabulary may be close to the labeling process or reflect treatment-seeking and self-disclosure rather than depression itself.
Quotation, lyric, joke, news, and third-person detection was heuristic; Portuguese slang, sarcasm, code-switching, and figurative language can create false positives or negatives.
Posts had source order but no usable timestamps, so temporal features represent lexical orientation rather than verified changes over calendar time.
The development set is imbalanced and associations are observational; none of these signals establishes causality or clinical diagnosis.

caveats: Pronouns and verb forms can occur in quotations, replies, lyrics, or discussion of others.
The feature is linguistic self-focus, not a clinical measure.
findings.evidence_summary: The diagnosed group uses substantially more singular self-reference and first-person verb morphology. This survives user-level normalization and a first-100-post sensitivity check.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use singular self-reference as a broad stylistic feature, preferably together with affect or agency; do not treat pronoun counts alone as evidence of lived symptoms.

negative_results: First-person plural language was not elevated: 3.26% of posts for diagnosed users versus 3.43% for controls, with controls higher in three of four folds.
Past-oriented vocabulary showed no stable difference: 13.14% versus 13.33% of posts, with mixed fold directions.
Social-connectedness vocabulary was mixed and nearly universal: 12.83% versus 12.54%, diagnosed higher in folds 0–1 but controls higher in folds 2 and 4.
Absolutist-language rates were close: 13.18% versus 12.72%; prevalence was too high for strong user-level discrimination.
Certainty did not decrease in diagnosed users; certainty markers were slightly higher (12.94% versus 12.28%), while uncertainty was also higher.
Broad negative-affect vocabulary alone had only a modest gap (7.17% versus 6.26%); the stronger signal was negative affect combined with self-reference.
